statement: For small swings, a pendulum's period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). It depends on length and g only, not on mass or amplitude.
worked_example: L = 1.0 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2: T = 2 pi sqrt(1.0/9.8) = 2.0 s, whether the bob is 100 g or 400 g.
analogy: A playground swing keeps the same rhythm whether a child or an adult sits on it.
steps: Identify the restoring system (string length and g).
Write T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
Check which quantities changed: only L or g change T.
wrong_idea: A heavier bob or a bigger swing takes longer.
why_wrong: Extra mass needs extra force, and gravity supplies exactly that extra force, so acceleration is unchanged. A bigger swing has a longer path but the bob moves faster on it.

statement: In SHM, a = -omega^2 x: acceleration is largest at the extremes, speed is largest at the centre, and total energy is E = (1/2) k A^2.
worked_example: E = 8 mJ at A = 2 cm. At A = 4 cm: E = 8 mJ x (4/2)^2 = 32 mJ.
analogy: A ball thrown up stops at the top but gravity never switches off; the spring does the same at each turning point.
steps: Find the displacement x.
Use a = -omega^2 x for acceleration.
Use E = (1/2) k A^2 for energy; it scales with A squared.
wrong_idea: At the extremes the body is at rest, so its acceleration is zero.
why_wrong: Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration. The spring force is largest at the largest displacement.

statement: A wave is a chain of particles each doing SHM in place. The medium fixes the speed (v = sqrt(T/mu) on a string); the source fixes the frequency; lambda = v/f.
worked_example: v = 12 m/s on a string. f = 4 Hz gives lambda = 3.0 m; f = 8 Hz gives lambda = 1.5 m. v stays 12 m/s.
analogy: A stadium wave: each fan stands and sits in place, but the wave runs around the stand.
steps: Ask what the medium sets: v.
Ask what the source sets: f.
Compute lambda = v/f.
wrong_idea: Shaking faster makes the wave travel faster.
why_wrong: Speed depends on tension and mass per unit length. Shaking faster packs the crests closer (smaller lambda) at the same speed.

statement: Overlapping waves add displacement point by point. Two close frequencies give beats at f_beat = |f1 - f2|, heard at pitch (f1 + f2)/2.
worked_example: 256 Hz and 260 Hz: f_beat = |260 - 256| = 4 beats per second, pitch 258 Hz.
analogy: Two people walking with slightly different step rates fall into and out of step at a regular rhythm.
steps: Find the difference of the two frequencies.
Take its absolute value: that is the beat frequency.
Energy is not lost at quiet moments; it is redistributed in time.
wrong_idea: The beat frequency is half the difference.
why_wrong: The envelope cosine has frequency (f1 - f2)/2, but loudness peaks at both its maximum and minimum, so beats come twice as often.

statement: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
worked_example: You stand 2.0 m from a mirror: image is 2.0 m behind it, so 4.0 m from you.
analogy: The mirror is a window into an identical room behind the wall.
steps: Measure the object distance to the mirror.
Place the image the same distance behind.
Distance from object to image is twice that.
wrong_idea: Stepping back lets you see more of yourself.
why_wrong: The ray from your feet to your eye always meets the mirror halfway up, whatever the distance, so the visible portion is fixed.

statement: A concave mirror forms a real inverted image when the object is beyond F, and a virtual erect magnified image when the object is inside F. Use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = -v/u (Cartesian signs).
worked_example: u = -10 cm, f = -15 cm: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 + 1/10 = 1/30, v = +30 cm (behind the mirror); m = -v/u = +3, virtual and erect.
analogy: A shaving mirror magnifies your face upright up close, but flips distant objects.
steps: Write u and f with signs (both negative in front of a concave mirror).
Solve 1/v = 1/f - 1/u.
Positive v means behind the mirror: virtual.
wrong_idea: A real image only exists if a screen is there.
why_wrong: The rays meet at the image point with or without a screen; the screen only scatters the light so you can see it from many directions.

statement: Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium. A convex lens converges light; every part of it forms the whole image. Use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u.
analogy: Covering half a window dims the room but you still see the whole garden.
steps: Write u (negative) and f (positive for convex).
Solve 1/v = 1/f + 1/u.
Find m = v/u; negative m means inverted.
wrong_idea: Covering half the lens removes half the image.
why_wrong: Rays from every object point pass through every part of the lens, so the uncovered half still forms the full image with less light.

statement: Two coherent slits make fringes of width beta = lambda D / d. Dark fringes are where the waves arrive half a wavelength out of step and cancel.
analogy: Two speakers playing the same tone give loud and quiet spots across a room.
steps: Check the sources are coherent (same source split in two).
Use beta = lambda D / d.
Bigger d means narrower fringes.
wrong_idea: Dark fringes are shadows where no light arrives.
why_wrong: Light from both slits does arrive there; it cancels. Block one slit and the dark spot gets brighter.

statement: A single slit of width a spreads light into a central band of width 2 lambda D / a. Narrower slits spread light more.
analogy: Water waves fan out widely through a narrow harbour gap but stay as a straight band through a wide one.
steps: Identify the slit width a.
Central band width = 2 lambda D / a.
Halving a doubles the width.
wrong_idea: Covering one slit of a double slit just dims the fringes.
why_wrong: Fringes come from two coherent waves interfering; with one slit there is only its own broad diffraction pattern.
